newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Scepticism over news Pol Pot on run after murders.
newsitem.headline: Scepticism over news Pol Pot on run after murders.

text.p: Reports that reviled Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot, who reigned over Cambodia's "killing fields," had fled his last rebel stronghold were greeted with scepticism by analysts and officials on Friday. While there was little consensus on the fate of Pol Pot and other top leaders, analysts and officials agreed that the movement that terrorised Cambodia during its 1975-1979 rule was indeed reeling from serious and violent internal strife.
Co-Premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh said that after decades of civil war he hoped lasting peace was finally in sight with the apparent departure of one of the 20th century's most notorious figures.
"I really hope this is the end of the life of the Khmer Rouge because Pol Pot can't live any longer," Ranariddh told reporters at a school opening ceremony on Friday morning.

Earlier, he said an ailing Pol Pot brutally murdered his longtime comrade-in-arms and defence chief Son Sen as well as 11 of his family members. Pol Pot apparently suspected Son Sen of forging an alliance with Cambodia's second prime minister Hun Sen.
Pol Pot then abducted Khieu Samphan, a senior official of the Khmer Rouge and other hostages and fled with 200 loyal fighters, Ranariddh said.
Virtually all the rest of Pol Pot's estimated 2,000 troops had defected to the government, he told reporters.
Hours after his comments, reports emerged of fighting between forces loyal to Pol Pot and breakaway rebels in Anlong Veng, but the location of "Brother Number One," remained a mystery.
Analysts cautioned against believing any unconfirmed reports about the shadowy Pol Pot, who remains the movement's most powerful figure and spiritual leader.
He has been reported dead at least twice and in the past week alone, conflicting reports have placed him in Anlong Veng, Bangkok or China, they said.

Cambodian officials, analysts and Thai military officials close to the issue said they were sceptical that Pol Pot had fled, citing his long-standing ties with the top leaders of the movement and the loyalty of his troops.
"I'm sceptical. Pol Pot is well-liked by his commanders and soldiers. I don't see any reason why this would happen," said one scholar of the Khmer Rouge. "It's unlikely he fled."
"This is voodoo-land," said a diplomat in Phnom Penh. "It's all very dramatic and hard to believe."

What was more believable, said analysts, was that the rebels wished to make it appear that Pol Pot was gone, making any peace agreements with lower level hard-line troops more palatable to the Cambodian population.

"I think the report is part of the Khmer Rouge strategy to make these three most hated men disappear...," said one Cambodian official speaking from Bangkok in apparent reference to Pol Pot, Son Sen and Khieu Samphan.

Pol Pot would have few options if he did flee, the analysts added, noting the rough jungle terrain around Anlong Veng and the fact that Thailand and China have said they would not allow him to go into exile in their nations.
While analysts suspected that reports of Pol Pot's flight might be simply misinformation, they agreed that the rebel movement was clearly in trouble.
"Obviously there is trouble in Anlong Veng... I would tend to believe that Son Sen had drifted away...and Pol Pot has neutralised him," said another expert on the Khmer Rouge.
Analysts said the Khmer Rouge has historically been plagued by distrust among its members, citing the murder of hundreds of its own during the waning years of their regime.
Last August, senior rebel Ieng Sary, brother-in-law of Pol Pot and former foreign minister under the Khmer Rouge regime, broke with rebels and thousands of defections followed.
Now fewer than 2,000 rebels are thought to remain in Anlong Veng, and given their internal problems they may prove to be their own worst enemy, analysts said.
